chapter: Fats Waller, Zululand and the ideal band
title: The ideal band and integrated bands
summary: He describes integrated bands and names players he would want, empathy and compassion.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: This question may sound like a static one but I don't think it is really because I think we're all dreamers. And I think that when we stop dreaming we're in trouble. (LAUGHTER). So if I may ask you to be a dreamer for a moment I will pose this question to you. We have literary Utopias and I'm certain musicians must have musical Utopias in

mind sometimes. So that if at this point you could put together your ideal band or your ideal group or whatever you want to call it, your ensemble. And if you could play under the circumstances or in the places that you would like to play. In other words, the places you would dream of. The most ideal set up and the ideal players.
I'm sure, but, and you're such a beautiful person, you love so many people I know I'm putting you on but I still think that there may be a few people who you would just have to have.

That's a little different. But it's alright. I've always had integrated bands for, oh gosh, I don't know how many years now, years and years. But it's not a matter of, to me of hiring black or white or anything like that. It's a matter of musicianship and a person, the individual, what kind of a person is he? That is, oh, that's a big thing because in music you must have empathy and compassion with each other.

Empathy of feeling together, just like we're talking. You must do the same thing with a band and musically because you must feel together and think together. Same as a conversation. And this is an important thing. Now I usually have a six piece band. I usually like to try to get three black and three white. This represents America to me. And it represents music also. Well you can't always do that because some guy's working or it's not enough money or whatever it is, but I usually come pretty close. Maybe it's four and two, and sometimes it's five and one. (LAUGHTER). And sometimes I have five black guys and one me you know. (LAUGHTER).

And I always say, what the hell am I doing here? I say it when I kid around. We have a ball. But I noticed two trombone players that I would love to have right off the bat and that Tyree Glenn or Vic Dickenson. Those two guys are so individual. They are beautiful guys. Oh, they're lovely. And then there's Herb Hall on clarinet, Edmond Hall's brother. And of course, Buster Bailey is gone, he's passed away.
